alt: Weighted graph of ten towns with the twelve road distances from the lesson; Dijkstra's shortest path from Harare to Bulawayo is H, C, K, G, B with total distance 100 + 60 + 140 + 165 = 465
caption: Figure: the town graph with the shortest path from Harare to Bulawayo highlighted

alt: Binary search for 45 in the 12 sorted values: the middle items compared are Data[6] = 31, Data[9] = 52, Data[7] = 38 and Data[8] = 45, so the range shrinks 12, 6, 2, 1 and 45 is found in 4 comparisons
caption: Figure: the range of the search shrinking at each step

alt: Bubble sort of 34, 12, 27, 9, 41, 18: after pass 1 the largest value 41 is at the end, passes 2 and 3 fix 34 and then 27, and pass 4 makes two comparisons with no swaps so the sort stops; 14 comparisons and 8 swaps in all
caption: Figure: the array after each pass of the bubble sort, with comparisons and swaps

alt: Flowchart that counts positive numbers: start, Count set to 0, input a number, if it is 0 output Count and end, otherwise if it is greater than 0 add 1 to Count, and loop back to the input; for 4, -2, 7, 0 the output is 2
caption: Figure: the flowchart for counting the positive numbers entered before 0

alt: Fetch stage for the instruction LDM #20 stored at address 100: 1 the address in the PC (100) is copied to the MAR, 2 the PC increases to 101, 3 the instruction at that address travels on the data bus into the MDR, 4 it is copied to the CIR
caption: Figure: the four fetch steps, with the register contents for the program stored from address 100

alt: Harvard architecture: separate instruction memory and data memory each have their own buses to the processor, so an instruction can be fetched while data is read or written
caption: Figure: the Harvard architecture, with separate memories and buses for instructions and data

alt: Von Neumann architecture: the processor (clock, ALU, control unit, registers PC, CIR, MAR, MDR and ACC) is joined to a single main memory holding both instructions and data by one address bus (one-way), one data bus and one control bus (two-way)
caption: Figure: the Von Neumann model with one memory and one set of buses

alt: Floating-point layout for 13.25: the 8-bit mantissa 01101010 has the binary point after the sign bit and equals 0.828125, the 4-bit exponent 0100 is 4, so the value is 0.828125 times 16 = 13.25
caption: Figure: 13.25 as mantissa 01101010 and exponent 0100

alt: Two's complement place values for 8 bits: 11010011 is -128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1 = -45 and 10110100 is -128 + 32 + 16 + 4 = -76, because the leftmost bit is worth -128
caption: Figure: reading 11010011 (−45) and 10110100 (−76) with a left-most place value of −128

alt: E-R diagram of the library in crow's foot notation: one Category has many Books, one Member has many Loans and one Book has many Loans, so Loan is the link table holding the foreign keys MemberID and BookID
caption: Figure: the library E-R diagram with primary and foreign keys

alt: Binary search tree built by inserting 45, 28, 63, 17, 36, 52, 71, 40: smaller keys go left and larger keys go right, so 40 is the right child of 36; an in-order walk gives 17, 28, 36, 40, 45, 52, 63, 71
caption: Figure: the tree built from the keys in the order 45, 28, 63, 17, 36, 52, 71, 40

alt: Circular queue of five places after the lesson's operations: places [1] to [5] hold T6, T7, T3, T4 and T5, Front = 3 and Rear = 2, Count = 5 so it is full, and T6 and T7 reused the places emptied by T1 and T2
caption: Figure: the final state of the circular queue, with Front and Rear

alt: Linked list after adding Rudo: following Next from Start = 2 gives Chipo, Farai, Nyasha, Rudo, Tatenda, null; only Next[1] changed from 3 to 5 and Rudo's Next is 3, so no items moved
caption: Figure: the names in alphabetical order; Nyasha and Rudo (amber) are the nodes whose pointers changed

alt: Linked list after deleting Rudo and inserting Nyasha: from Start = 4 the pointers give Anesu, Farai, Nyasha, Tendai, Zodwa, null; Nyasha reused the freed node 3 and no item moved
caption: Figure: the six-node list after the last operation; Farai and Nyasha (amber) are the nodes whose pointers changed

alt: Stack of six places after push 12, push 7, push 20, pop, push 5, pop, pop: the pops return 20, 5 and 7 (last in, first out) and the stack finally holds only 12 with Top = 1
caption: Figure: the stack after each of seven push and pop operations

alt: Weighted graph with vertices A to E: undirected edges A-B 4, A-C 2, B-D 5, C-D 8 and D-E 3; below, the directed version with one-way edges A to B 4, B to D 5, C to A 2 and D to E 3
caption: Figure: the undirected weighted graph and the directed graph used in the lesson

alt: Four-variable Karnaugh map: the four corner cells form one wrap-around group giving NOT B AND NOT D, and the centre four cells give B AND D, so X is 1 when B and D are equal
caption: Figure: a 4-variable K-map with a corner group and a centre group

alt: Three-variable Karnaugh map with rows A and columns BC in Gray order: the four 1s in the first and last columns wrap around to give NOT C, the pair at A=1, B=1 gives A AND B, so X = (A AND B) OR (NOT C)
caption: Figure: grouping the 1s on a 3-variable K-map, including a wrap-around group

alt: Logic circuit for X = (A AND B) OR (NOT C): A and B feed an AND gate giving P, C feeds a NOT gate giving Q, and P and Q feed an OR gate giving X
caption: Figure: the circuit for X = (A AND B) OR (NOT C), with the gate outputs P and Q labelled

alt: Logic circuit for M = G AND (S OR R): the start button S and the remote R feed an OR gate, and its output P goes to an AND gate with the guard signal G, so the motor M runs only when G is 1 and S or R is 1
caption: Figure: the conveyor circuit M = G AND (S OR R)

alt: Full adder: two half adders and an OR gate; the first half adder adds A and B to give P and Q, the second adds P and the carry in Cin to give the sum S and R, and Cout = Q OR R
caption: Figure: a full adder built from two half adders and an OR gate

alt: The seven logic gate symbols with their truth tables: NOT inverts; AND is 1 only for 11; OR is 0 only for 00; NAND is 0 only for 11; NOR is 1 only for 00; XOR is 1 when A and B differ; XNOR is 1 when they are the same
caption: Figure: the NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR symbols, each with its truth table

alt: Half adder: an XOR gate gives the sum S and an AND gate gives the carry C from the same inputs A and B; 1 + 1 gives sum 0 and carry 1
caption: Figure: a half adder is one XOR gate (sum) and one AND gate (carry), with its truth table

alt: NAND gates can build every other gate: NOT is a NAND with joined inputs, AND is a NAND followed by a NAND used as NOT, and OR is two NAND-as-NOT gates feeding a third NAND
caption: Figure: NOT, AND and OR built from NAND gates only

alt: Four-stage ripple-carry adder adding 0110 and 0111: the carry out of each full adder is the carry in of the next stage to the left, giving the sum bits 1101 and a final carry out of 0
caption: Figure: a 4-stage ripple-carry adder working out 0110 + 0111 = 1101

alt: SR flip-flop built from two NOR gates whose outputs feed back to each other: S=1 sets Q to 1, R=1 resets Q to 0, S=R=0 holds the stored bit, and S=R=1 is not allowed
caption: Figure: an SR flip-flop from two cross-coupled NOR gates

alt: Two bank branches: laptops L1 and L2 join SwitchA (links 1 and 2), SwitchA joins RouterA (3), the WAN link 4 joins RouterA and RouterB, RouterB joins SwitchB (5), and SwitchB joins PC P1 (6) and Server S1 (7); the path from L1 to S1 uses links 1, 3, 4, 5 and 7
caption: Figure: the bank network with the path from Laptop L1 to Server S1 highlighted

alt: Encapsulation of the first 1460-byte piece of a file: TCP adds a 20-byte header (segment 1480 bytes), IP adds 20 bytes (packet 1500 bytes) and the link layer adds a 14-byte header and 4-byte trailer (frame 1518 bytes)
caption: Figure: each layer wraps the data in its own header, giving a segment, a packet and a frame

alt: Packet switching: a 4500-byte message becomes 5 packets of payload 1000, 1000, 1000, 1000 and 500 bytes, each with a 20-byte header and 4-byte trailer; they arrive in the order 2, 1, 3, 5, 4 and are put in order by packet number
caption: Figure: splitting a message into packets and reassembling them in order

alt: Four network topologies: bus (devices on one backbone), star (each device cabled to a central switch), full mesh (4 devices need 6 links) and hybrid (two stars whose switches are joined by a backbone)
caption: Figure: bus, star, mesh and hybrid topologies

alt: Gantt chart for first come first served: A runs 0 to 6, B 6 to 9, C 9 to 13 and D 13 to 15; the waiting times are 0, 5, 7 and 8, so the mean waiting time is 5
caption: Figure: the FCFS schedule for processes A, B, C and D

alt: Paging: logical address 4100 with 1024-byte pages is page 4, offset 4; the page table maps page 4 to frame 9, so the physical address is 9 x 1024 + 4 = 9220
caption: Figure: translating logical address 4100 to physical address 9220 through the page table

alt: Class diagram: the superclass Item has private Title and ItemID and methods NEW, GetTitle and Describe; subclasses Book (Pages) and Dvd (Minutes) inherit from Item and each overrides Describe
caption: Figure: Book and Dvd inherit from Item and override Describe

alt: State-transition diagram for a wallet PIN: from Start, OneWrong and TwoWrong a wrong PIN moves to the next state and three wrong PINs reach Blocked; a correct PIN from any of those three states goes to Menu; Blocked and Menu stay in the same state for any input
caption: Figure: states and transitions for the three-wrong-PINs rule

alt: Three-tier architecture of a results portal: the presentation tier on the user's device talks only to the application tier on the application server, which talks to the data tier on the database server
caption: Figure: the presentation, application and data tiers with the results-portal example

alt: Waterfall model: analysis, design, coding, testing and maintenance follow each other like steps, with the output of each stage flowing to the next
caption: Figure: the five stages of the waterfall model

alt: Symmetric encryption uses the same secret key to encrypt and decrypt; asymmetric encryption for confidentiality encrypts with the receiver's public key and only the receiver's private key can decrypt
caption: Figure: key use in symmetric and asymmetric encryption

alt: The four stages of compilation: lexical analysis turns source code into tokens and a symbol table, syntax analysis builds a parse tree, code generation produces intermediate or object code, and optimisation makes it faster or smaller; errors are found in the first two stages
caption: Figure: the four compilation stages and what each one produces

alt: Parse tree of Price * Qty + 15: the root is + with children the * node and 15, and the * node has children Price and Qty, so multiplication (lower in the tree) is carried out before the addition
caption: Figure: the parse tree for Price * Qty + 15

alt: Evaluating 8 4 + 3 * 10 5 / - with a stack: the stack goes 8; 8,4; 12; 12,3; 36; 36,10; 36,10,5; 36,2; and finally 34, because each operator replaces the top two values by their result
caption: Figure: the stack after each token of the postfix expression
